turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Tyler Nelson, date of birth: 3, 6, 1949, mrn, 385729. He is here today for ongoing management of rheumatoid arthritis. Last time he was here, he received a steroid injection in his right knee. Hello mr. Nelson, how are you?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Um, about the same as last time. My knee is still swollen.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: That was your right knee, correct? I take it the injection didn't help?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: It did, maybe for a couple of weeks.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: That's it? And is it still painful?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Yeah, it's pretty painful, and now the whole leg is getting swollen.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay, what would you say your pain level is?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: I mean, right now it's about a 3 or so, but, typically on a normal day it's around 6.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay, and its been swollen like that for how long now?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Since I was last here a couple weeks after that. So about, maybe two months now.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay, but before it was just the knee?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Yeah, the whole thing wasn't swollen like this, but I tried to wear compression socks a lot of the time, but it hasn't been helping.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay, okay, so that hasn't been working for you?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: I mean, it helps to some degree, but it's still swollen, especially around the knee.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Hmm. Has it been keeping you from doing things during the day?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Well, I slowed down a little bit, and I found a few things too fast. But when it really hurts, is when I've been sitting for a while, and then I have to try and get up. I'm so stiff getting up I have to use a cane to get my bearings. I mean, after a little bit, it loosens up, but that first getting up is real difficult.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Yeah, I can see, that makes sense. Have you been taking your medication regularly? Your on xeljanz right?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Yeah, the xr, I think its, uhm, 11 milligrams a day? Yeah, but I'm taking it everyday, and I'm also taking celebrex which I started maybe 2 months ago.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Yes, the 200mgs daily. How's that working for you?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Pretty good, up until it started swelling again.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay, well come sit over here, and if you could take of your socks and shoes, and we'll take a look at your knee. And just to let you know, I have a service now that writes my note about the visit, so you'll hear me call things out and describe what I see fully.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Okay, gotcha.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Right, so let's check your leg. Can you straighten it, and does it hurt?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Yeah, when I try to straighten it all the way it does.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay, range of motion slightly diminished. I'm going to press here, okay? And how about here, hmm, I see some pitting around the knee and ankle. Normal capillary refill in the toes. Does any of this area hurt?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Um, just kinda sore, like an old bruise?

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: So, I can feel that the knee is hot, and that means there's something going on, like some inflammation. So we can give you another steroid injection for that. I also want to get an x-ray of that knee, so we can see where all the swelling is coming from.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Yeah. Let's do it. Sounds go to me.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay, and did we set up physical therapy for you last time you were here?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Yeah, that was some years ago, but that was the other knee.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. So I think we'll set that up for you now. We'll also do an x-ray on that knee. I can send you for a physical therapy, and if nothing is helping, then we really might need to get a surgery consult to see what we can do with that knee.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Okay, sounds like a plan.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: All right, so for today we'll go ahead and we'll give you the steroid shot. I'll try to see if I can get a little bit of fluid out before I do give you the injection. There might be no fluid, but I'll see if I can get anything out regardless.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Okay. And that's a procedure you're going to do right now?

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Yep. Once we're done talking here, and as far as the edema in your legs, uh, we'll take an x-ray to look for the cause, but there is a lot you can do as well. The compression socks are a good start. Um, and also, do you eat a lot of salt?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: I mean, um, I mean I love my salty snacks.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. Well, salt does have a tendency to make your body hold on to water, reducing your salt intake could help with some of the swelling. You can also prop your feet up any time you get a chance, especially at night. And have you talked to your private care doctor about this at all?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: No, I figured I would just come here first.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. So I think, try some of those things out first, and if it doesn't help, definitely make an appointment with them, also, as you know, xeljanz is a high-risk medication, so we need to check your cmp levels every couple of months. So this time your levels are good, but do make sure to make an appointment for the blood work for next time.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: All right. I can do that. Thank you so much doc.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Yes, of course. Well let me go ahead and get supplies and we'll get to work on your knee. Fluid aspiration and steroid injection procedure. The risks, benefits, and alternatives were explained. The risks of steroid injection were explained, including, but not limited to: hypopigmentation, soft tissue atrophy, tendon ruptures, and transient hypoglycemia among others. Verbal consent was attained. The right knee was, uh, um, accessed through the lateral approach with 3 milliliters of initially clear fluid, then bloo- blood tinged fluid. Then the right knee was prepped in a standard-fashion. The right knee was injected with 80 milligrams of triamcinolone, and one milliliter of lidocaine. The procedure was tolerated well, with no complications. Post-procedure instructions were given. Patient will follow up with his pcp. Thank you.
